Sealand is an interesting place with a lot of creative potential, but it's always been hampered by being a magnet for kooks and bureaucrats with bugs up their asses. It was never some grand protest or demonstration. More of a family hobby project and novel vacation home where Roy Bates was chiefly seeking sovereignty so he could claim and do what he wanted with the long-abandoned military structure without being hassled. It's one of a group of Maunsell Forts that were abandoned in the '50s and became popular with the pirate radio movement in the '60s. They are remote, but not terribly difficult to access by small boat when the weather is good and so Roy Bates, himself in the pirate radio movement for a time, thought that since some of these were--back in the '70s'--outside of territorial waters it might be fun to claim one for his own, call it a principality, and make a novel home out of it. And, of course, the UK authorities compulsively overreacted to that as they do everything, and so it became a fight and a controversy for a time until someone in the government realized they were spending years and huge amounts of money bitching over an abandoned lump of concrete in the ocean some guy just wanted to have a little creative fun with.

You might wonder why anyone would want to live there, but it's not really that remote, it's big enough for a large comfortable home, and other sea forts have been made into nice luxury resorts. They offer an experience akin to a cruise liner without having to travel around. But the Bates family has never had the resources these resort projects have had and the much smaller scale and lofted structure of the Maunsell forts is a bigger adaptive reuse design challenge. Much could be done with it, but it's a difficult place to get materials and equipment too.

I've been involved with an organization that was trying to use Sealand as a setting for educational videos showcasing open source culture with a project called Sealand Multiversity --though it was a bit more art than education. I had hoped I could get support to demonstrate the modular building systems I've been developing there, as it takes a different logistics approach than the usual renovation project. Sadly, the project fizzled out quickly, perhaps in part because of Roy Bates' death around that time.
